subject: Architecture
title: Bauhaus: The School That Changed Design
description: A short lesson to help you apply Bauhaus: The School That Changed Design.

hook.text: In 1919, Walter Gropius opened a school in Weimar that united art, craft, and architecture.

buildup.text: Bauhaus taught that form follows function — no decoration for decoration's sake.

discovery.text: Students designed everything: furniture, lamps, typography, textiles, and entire buildings.

twist.text: The Nazis shut Bauhaus down in 1933, calling its clean modernism 'degenerate art.'

climax.text: Its teachers fled to America and spread Bauhaus ideas worldwide. The Nazis killed the school but not the movement.

punchline.text: A 14-year school changed how the entire world designs.

quiz.question: Why did the Nazis shut down the Bauhaus school?
options: It was too expensive for the government to fund
They considered its modernist style degenerate art
Students were involved in political protests

details.summary: The Bauhaus school (1919-1933) in Germany unified art, craft, and technology under one educational philosophy, producing the foundations of modern design.
details.whyItMatters: Bauhaus created the design language of the modern world. The clean lines, functional forms, and industrial materials we take for granted in everything from office chairs to apartment buildings originated in this single German school's 14-year.
takeaways: Unified art, craft, and technology in one design philosophy
Form follows function became the defining design principle
Its 14-year existence shaped the entire modern design world

faq.question: Why did the Bauhaus close?
faq.answer: The Nazis closed it in 1933, considering its internationalist aesthetic and leftist associations degenerate. Key faculty — including Gropius, Mies van der Rohe, and László Moholy-Nagy — emigrated to the United States, where they spread Bauhaus principles through American design education.

faq.question: What lasting impact did the Bauhaus have?
faq.answer: Its alumni defined modern architecture (Mies van der Rohe), industrial design (Marcel Breuer's tubular steel furniture), graphic design (Herbert Bayer's typography), and art education worldwide. The International Style of glass-and-steel buildings descends directly from Bauhaus principles.
